content: The use of triple antiretroviral therapy (ARVs) as recommended can reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV to less than 5%. The United Nations has outlined a comprehensive approach to preventing MTCT, which includes four key strategies: (1) primary prevention of HIV infection among women of childbearing age, (2) prevention of unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV, (3) prevention of HIV transmission from HIV-positive pregnant women to their infants, and (4) provision of appropriate treatment, care, and support for mothers living with HIV, their children, and families. The PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission) cascade tracks the sequence of interventions provided to mother-baby pairs, starting with identifying the total number of pregnant women, determining their HIV status, and offering HIV testing to male partners. It also includes the delivery of ARVs to HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women, early testing of exposed infants, and final determination of the infants' HIV status. Early treatment of HIV-infected infants and linkage to chronic HIV care for HIV-positive women are also critical components of the cascade. The continuum of HIV care and the expanded package of prevention and care services are integrated into PMTCT services for HIV-positive women and their exposed children. Recent WHO guidelines have simplified PMTCT ARV interventions, recommending that all HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women initiate triple ARVs and continue treatment at least through the MTCT risk period. Two options are available: Option B, where women stop ARVs after breastfeeding if not eligible for lifelong ART, and Option B+, where all HIV-positive women continue lifelong ART regardless of eligibility criteria. As countries adopt these guidelines, more women are receiving long-term ART, often in the form of a single-pill, fixed-dose combination. Health systems have adapted by integrating ART services into maternal and child health (MCH) clinics, decentralizing services, task-shifting, improving supply chains, strengthening linkages to chronic HIV care, and investing in laboratory capacity. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems must evolve to track long-term ART use and outcomes for HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women. This includes ensuring compatibility between PMTCT and ART monitoring systems, transferring patient records post-partum, and tracking ART services based on time since initiation rather than antenatal care visits. Toxicity monitoring is also essential to detect adverse reactions in pregnant women and infants receiving PMTCT services. Retention on ART and final HIV status determination for exposed infants are critical indicators of PMTCT program effectiveness. Countries must improve data collection during breastfeeding and validate the elimination of MTCT (eMTCT). Effective implementation requires robust M&E systems, integration of services, and targeted interventions for high-risk populations.
